result: ATF6α is a type-II transmembrane ER protein that functions as an ER stress sensor in the UPR. Upon ER stress, ATF6α traffics to the Golgi where it is cleaved by S1P and S2P, releasing ATF6α-N which translocates to the nucleus to activate cytoprotective target genes.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 describe well-established background knowledge about ATF6α biology, all supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These claims provide the foundational context for the study but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings from this manuscript.

result: The mechanisms regulating ATF6α retention in the ER, its release upon ER stress, its interaction with COPII machinery, and what aspect of the folding environment it senses remain unknown.
evaluation: Claims C8, C9, C14, C17, and C97 accurately describe gaps in knowledge that motivate this study. These statements establish the scientific context and rationale for the experimental work presented.

result: Ceapins selectively inhibit ATF6α processing by preventing its selection into COPII vesicles and retaining it in ER foci. Ceapins induce rapid ATF6α clustering, and removing the trafficking requirement restores cleavage, indicating that oligomeric state regulates ATF6α trafficking and activation.
evaluation: Claims C22-C27 present the core findings of the manuscript, supported by extensive experimental data including microscopy (Figures 1-6), Western blots (Figure 5), and brefeldin A experiments. The conclusion about oligomeric state regulation (C27) is a reasonable inference from the clustering data and brefeldin A rescue experiments.

result: In unstressed cells, GFP-ATF6α localizes to the ER, but upon ER stress translocates to the nucleus. Active Ceapin-A7 (but not inactive A5) prevents nuclear translocation and induces discrete GFP-ATF6α foci that persist for up to 24 hours, even in the absence of ER stress.
evaluation: Claims C29-C36 are well-supported by microscopy data in Figure 1 and supplements, showing clear differences between active and inactive Ceapin analogs. The quantification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and time-course data strengthen these observations. The foci represent uncleaved ATF6α as confirmed by reference to the accompanying manuscript.

result: ATF6α foci are observed in cells subjected to ER stress alone at later time points corresponding to when ATF6α signaling attenuation occurs, consistent with prior observations that ATF6α signaling attenuates during prolonged ER stress.
evaluation: Claims C37, C104, and C105 are supported by microscopy data (Figure 1J, Video 2) and citations to prior work (Haze et al., 2001; Rutkowski et al., 2006). This observation connects the Ceapin-induced phenotype to a natural regulatory mechanism.

result: Ceapin-induced GFP-ATF6α foci are reversible. Washout of Ceapins leads to rapid foci dissolution, and the same ATF6α molecules are redistributed in the ER. After washout, cells respond to ER stress with normal kinetics, demonstrating that Ceapins are reversible inhibitors that restore an activatable pool of ATF6α.
evaluation: Claims C38-C43 are strongly supported by washout experiments (Figure 2, Videos 7-13) including cycloheximide controls that demonstrate the same molecules are redistributed. The restoration of ER stress responsiveness after washout (C41) provides functional validation of reversibility.

result: In unstressed cells, GFP-ATF6α shows little overlap with Golgi marker giantin, but upon ER stress shows clear co-localization, enhanced by S1P inhibitor treatment. Ceapin-A1 prevents this Golgi localization, suggesting ATF6α is not cleaved because it does not traffic to the Golgi.
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 are well-supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 3A-D). The S1P inhibitor control (C46-C47) is particularly important as it shows expected Golgi accumulation when cleavage is blocked, contrasting with Ceapin treatment. The inference in C49 is reasonable given the data.

result: Using 3xFLAG-ATF6α, the same trafficking patterns are observed: ER localization in unstressed cells, movement out of the ER upon stress, and Ceapin-A1-induced foci formation along ER tubules that prevent Golgi co-localization. This demonstrates that foci formation is independent of the tag and reflects an intrinsic ATF6α property.
evaluation: Claims C50-C55 are supported by immunofluorescence data using a different tag (3xFLAG) in different cells (293 T-REx) (Figure 3E-K). The consistency across different tags and cell types strengthens the conclusion that this is an intrinsic ATF6α property (C55).

result: After prolonged ER stress (2.4 hr), GFP-ATF6α shows Golgi localization, but in the presence of active Ceapins, foci remain on ER tubules with minimal Golgi co-localization. This effect is consistent across different cell types and ATF6α variants.
evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by extended time-course immunofluorescence data (Figure 3M-P). The consistency across cell types and tags (C58) is a reasonable inference from the combined data in Figure 3.

result: Endogenous ATF6α in unstressed cells is found in small foci distributed over the ER network, not evenly distributed. Upon ER stress, endogenous ATF6α co-localizes with Golgi markers and accumulates in the nucleus (p<0.0001). Ceapin-A7 blocks this, retaining ATF6α in enlarged ER foci, demonstrating that endogenous ATF6α phenocopies tagged variants and is naturally clustered in foci.
evaluation: Claims C59-C66 are strongly supported by immunofluorescence of endogenous ATF6α (Figure 4) with statistical quantification (Figure 4E, p<0.0001). The observation that endogenous ATF6α is already in foci (C59, C66) is a novel and important finding that differs from overexpressed tagged proteins.

result: Brefeldin A treatment fuses ER and Golgi compartments, relocalizing S1P and S2P to the ER. Under these conditions, ATF6α-N is produced even in the presence of active Ceapins (but not with S1P inhibitor or inactive Ceapin-A5). This demonstrates that Ceapins do not convert ATF6α to an uncleavable form, but rather inhibit cleavage by preventing trafficking to the protease-containing compartment.
evaluation: Claims C68-C76 are strongly supported by Western blot data (Figure 5A-B) showing differential effects of Ceapins versus S1P inhibitor under brefeldin A treatment. This is a critical experiment that definitively demonstrates the mechanism of Ceapin action. The logic is sound and the controls are appropriate.

result: In unstressed cells, minimal overlap exists between GFP-ATF6α and ER exit site markers (SEC16/SEC31A). Upon ER stress, overlap increases, consistent with ATF6α passing through ER exit sites. Active Ceapins produce foci non-overlapping with ER exit sites, while inactive Ceapin-A5 does not prevent co-localization. Live imaging confirms GFP-ATF6α foci remain distinct from ER exit site marker mRFP-p125A in Ceapin-treated cells.
evaluation: Claims C77-C82 are well-supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 6A-E) with quantification (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and live imaging (Figure 6H-I). The statistical analysis shows significant differences. However, the manuscript notes that exposure times differ between conditions, which could affect quantitative comparisons.

result: Ceapins do not block COPII-mediated trafficking generally, as SREBP and ATF6β trafficking are not inhibited. Instead, Ceapins selectively prevent ATF6α from being selected as cargo to leave the ER during ER stress.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84 are supported by data from the accompanying manuscript showing SREBP and ATF6β are not inhibited, combined with the ER exit site data from this manuscript. The selectivity is a key finding that argues against general trafficking defects.

result: Ceapins inhibit an early step in ATF6α activation—its selection as cargo to leave the ER—by clustering it in foci that do not engage with ER exit sites. Ceapins no longer inhibit ATF6α when the trafficking requirement is removed by brefeldin A, unlike S1P inhibitor which works regardless of localization. This demonstrates Ceapins do not create an uncleavable form of ATF6α.
evaluation: Claims C85-C89 synthesize the major findings and are well-supported by the combined data from Figures 1-6. The brefeldin A experiment (C87) is particularly important for establishing the mechanism. The logic connecting the observations is sound.

result: Ceapin-mediated inhibition is selective for ATF6α without inhibiting ATF6β, providing the first evidence of differences in activation mechanisms between these highly similar proteins that were previously thought equivalent in their stress-sensing and trafficking mechanisms, despite having highly conserved lumenal domains.
evaluation: Claims C90-C93 are supported by data from the accompanying manuscript and represent an important conceptual advance. The selectivity between ATF6α and ATF6β is surprising given their similarity (C93) and challenges prior assumptions (C92).

result: Ceapins do not interfere with SREBP signaling in response to cholesterol depletion, demonstrating that stress-sensing, cargo selection, and ER-Golgi transport are not generally affected by the drug.
evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by data from the accompanying manuscript. This selectivity is important for establishing that Ceapins act specifically on ATF6α rather than causing general cellular dysfunction.

result: All active Ceapin analogs tested induced ATF6α foci formation, while inactive analogs either did not induce foci or induced unstable foci that quickly disassembled. Dissolution of foci after washout restored ER stress-induced transport to the Golgi.
evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are supported by data across multiple figures showing structure-activity relationships. The correlation between biological activity and foci formation/stability strengthens the mechanistic model.

result: Endogenous ATF6α in unstressed cells exists in foci, suggesting the resting ER-retained state is an oligomer or higher-order complex. The model proposes that activation involves shifting equilibrium from oligomer to monomer (transport-competent), while attenuation shifts it back. Ceapins prevent formation of the transport-competent form and engage normal retention/attenuation mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C103-C109 present a mechanistic model supported by the endogenous ATF6α foci observation (C103, Figure 4) and the Ceapin effects. The model is reasonable given the data, though it remains somewhat speculative. The connection to natural attenuation mechanisms is supported by the observation of foci during prolonged ER stress.

result: ATF6α exists in monomeric and oligomeric forms in the ER, but only monomeric form is found in the Golgi. Both trafficking and oligomerization are regulated by the lumenal domain. The model proposes that the lumenal sensor domain responds to ER stress by converting from oligomer to monomer, transmitting information across the membrane to initiate COPII interactions.
evaluation: Claims C110-C112 integrate prior work (C110, citing Nadanaka et al., 2007) with the current findings. The model (C112) is speculative but consistent with the data and provides a mechanistic framework. The transmembrane signaling aspect is supported by analogy to other systems (C113-C114).

result: The high selectivity of Ceapins suggests they act by binding to ATF6α or an ATF6α-dedicated accessory factor. The proposed model is that Ceapins stabilize an oligomeric state that is not transport-competent, potentially by burying the COPII interaction interface. Ceapins may act as antagonists to prevent misfolded protein binding and stabilize ATF6α in its inactive state.
evaluation: Claims C96, C98, C99, and C119 are speculative models about Ceapin's molecular mechanism. While the selectivity data (C96) supports the idea of a specific target, the direct binding target and detailed mechanism (C98, C99, C119) remain unproven. These are reasonable hypotheses that require additional biochemical and structural studies for validation.

result: The lumenal domain of ATF6α (ATF6α-LD) dictates its localization and is sufficient to sense ER stress. Attaching ATF6α-LD to Sec22 confers stress-regulated trafficking, demonstrating that ATF6α-LD is ATF6α's stress-sensor and regulates its trafficking.
evaluation: Claims C10-C13 describe prior work (citing Chen et al., 2002; Schindler and Schekman, 2009; Sato et al., 2011) that establishes the role of the lumenal domain. These are well-established findings that provide important context for the current study.

result: The COPII coat machinery required for ATF6α trafficking is positioned on the cytosolic side of the ER membrane, requiring signal transmission from the ER lumen to the cytosol for ATF6α activation.
evaluation: Claims C15-C16 describe established cell biology (citing Schindler and Schekman, 2009; Nadanaka et al., 2004) that frames the mechanistic question addressed by this study.

result: SREBP has a trafficking mechanism involving INSIG (retention factor) and SCAP (transport factor), where SCAP senses cholesterol and regulates interactions with both INSIG and COPII coat. SREBP itself neither senses the signal nor interacts with trafficking machinery. A similar ATF6α-dedicated accessory factor may remain to be discovered.
evaluation: Claims C18-C20 describe the well-established SREBP/SCAP/INSIG system (citing Brown and Goldstein, 2009; Sun et al., 2007; Motamed et al., 2011) as an analogy. Claim C21 is speculative about potential undiscovered ATF6α factors, which is reasonable given the SREBP precedent.

result: There is precedence for conformational changes on one side of the membrane leading to changes on the other side in signaling proteins (SCAP, EGFR) and for conformational epitopes regulating COPII trafficking (Sec22, Kir2.1).
evaluation: Claims C113-C114 cite relevant prior work establishing precedents for the proposed mechanisms. These provide important context for the model but are not new findings from this study.

result: ATF6α activation correlates with BiP release, but there is also evidence for direct ligand binding activation (e.g., thrombospondin in cardiac cells). These mechanisms are not mutually exclusive, as shown for IRE1. ATF6α may bind misfolded proteins directly as ligands to activate signaling.
evaluation: Claims C115-C118 discuss prior work on ATF6α activation mechanisms (citing Shen et al., 2002, 2005; Lynch et al., 2012; Gardner and Walter, 2011; Pincus et al., 2010). These provide context for interpreting the Ceapin mechanism but are not new findings. Claim C118 is somewhat speculative.

result: Ceapins are named after the Irish verb 'ceap,' meaning 'to trap,' based on their mode of action corralling ATF6α into ER-restricted foci.
evaluation: Claim C28 is a nomenclature explanation that is directly stated and appropriate given the demonstrated mechanism.

result: Ceapins may further stabilize ATF6α foci, trapping ATF6α in the ER and preventing its Golgi trafficking and nuclear translocation.
evaluation: Claim C67 is a speculative statement about mechanism that is consistent with the data showing endogenous ATF6α is already in foci and Ceapins enhance this. This is a reasonable interpretation.
